per_window.ps-ns: dynamic_in_window (J6, r3): at 298 K in phosphate buffer the free protein has more fast backbone motion than the complex in the R59-E62 and V76/D77 portal loops, and the K101 betaG-betaH loop is flexible; mean NOE 0.82 ± 0.05, tauc 10.4 ns, no order parameters. Bound state kept apart: K101 loop still flexible (J7, r4), portal-loop motion quenched (J8, r3/r4).
per_window.us-ms: dynamic_in_window: free CRABP2 at 298 K, pH 7.4, 1.0 mM shows exchange across the portal and gap regions; a 16-residue core group fits kex 320 ± 40 s-1, pB 0.2 ± 0.03 (J1, r5), further residues exchange at similar but unshared rates (J2, r6), and 14 amides are broadened beyond assignment (J3, r9, indirect). With atRA the core process is not detected (J4, r7); a residual fluctuation at nine residues of the complex is unresolved because it overlaps the dimer interface (J5, r8). Single temperature, single paper.
per_window.slower_than_ms: not_measured (J14): HDX-MS, EPR/DEER, FRET, time-resolved and multitemperature structural methods and CEST were searched with no hits.
per_window.undetermined: Free protein: 1998 abstract reports weak or missing pocket HSQC peaks (J9, r1) and a disordered apo NMR ensemble at A32-P39 and T57-E62 with a wider entrance than the holo crystal (J10, r2), both unresolved. Apo 2FS6 and holo 2FR3 crystal pockets are near-identical (J11, r12, structure_only). The complex self-associates (Kd about 1.0 mM), an intermolecular process (J12, r10). SPR atRA kon/koff are binding kinetics (J13, r11). Not judged: r13-r15 (retinal Schiff-base fluorescence lifetimes in engineered KFVQ mutants at pH 3; chromophore photophysics), r16 (MD of the engineered M9 mutant), r17 (zonal-elution transient CRABP-II/RAR-gamma encounter of a His-tagged construct; partner binding), r18 (cellular photocrosslinking to NR2F1; contact capture), r19 (bound-ligand NOE conformation, abstract; ligand, not protein), r20 (CRABP-I paralog ligand motion, abstract).

protein_summary.wt_apo_answer: Yes: at 298 K (pH 7.4, 20 mM sodium phosphate, 150 mM NaCl, 1.0 mM protein) free human CRABP2 exchanges on the microsecond-millisecond scale across its portal and gap regions; a core group (K8, L19, L22, K30-A32, R59, E73, Q74, V76, T114, T131, Y134, plus a misnumbered 'Thr51-Ile53') fits one two-state process with kex 320 ± 40 s-1 and a minor-state population of 0.2 ± 0.03, the minor state differs from the atRA-bound structure but is otherwise unknown, and atRA suppresses the process; one paper, one temperature.
protein_summary.deposition_readback: None: the input lists no BMRB id and outputs/deposition/CRABP2.json does not exist. The 2019 paper verified the apo assignments of BMRB 4186.
open_conflicts: Apo pocket structure: the 1998 abstract reports a disordered apo NMR ensemble (A32-P39, T57-E62) with a wider ligand entrance than the holo crystal (r2), while the 2019 paper finds the apo 2FS6 and holo 2FR3 crystal pockets near-identical (r12); the restraint-scarcity reading of the 1998 ensemble is a row caveat, not a statement of either paper. Not a conflict of judgments (different methods, no rate), but the structure of the exchanging state stays open.

Core-group numbering: the 2019 text lists 'Thr51-Ile53' (betaC), but entry positions 51-53 are Y51-I52-K53 (T54 follows); Table S1 was not retrieved, so these positions are left out of J1 and J4 (r5, r7).
questions_for_gina: Which sample is the RelaxDB CRABP2 entry: the 2019 Biochemistry R1/R2/NOE set (900 MHz, 298 K, pH 7.4 phosphate, 1.0 mM apo), or another deposition? The input lists no BMRB id.

Which three residues does 'Thr51-Ile53' in the 2019 core group mean? No Thr-x-Ile stretch exists near betaC in the entry sequence (D48-T49-F50-Y51-I52-K53-T54); Table S1 of that paper would settle it.
protein_summary.buffer_note: All 2019 NMR relaxation, CPMG and assignment samples (r3-r9) used 20 mM sodium phosphate pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM DTT, 10% D2O, 1.0 mM protein, 298 K; no phosphate-free control, but no row identifies CRABP2 as a phosphate binder. The concentration series (r10) used pH 6.8, 50 mM NaCl, 0.5 mM TCEP. The atRA complex self-associates (apparent Kd about 1.0 ± 0.2 mM), so the 1.0 mM bound-state relaxation and residual dispersion include dimer contributions; the authors report no concentration-dependent CSPs for free CRABP2, and the 1998 abstract calls apo-CRABPII largely monomeric, so the apo exchange is not attributed to dimerisation. Only one temperature (298 K) was measured. The 2019 supplement (Table S1, Figs. S1-S6) was not retrieved.

detection.kex: 320 ± 40 s-1 (shared fit of the core group)

judgments.reason: At 298 K free CRABP2 shows microsecond-millisecond exchange in the portal and gap regions, and a core group of 13 mappable residues fits one two-state process with kex 320 ± 40 s-1 and pB 0.2 ± 0.03; the authors' CPMG shifts do not match the atRA-bound shifts, so the minor state is not the ligand-bound structure, and its own structure is unknown.
judgments.function_link: The authors conclude the fluctuation is not an opening step needed for atRA binding (binding is limited by atRA release from detergent), and propose that it matters for regulation because the nuclear-localisation residues K20, R29, K30, the RAR-binding surface and the dimer surface all fluctuate in the free protein and are quenched by atRA.

detection.detection_window: 15N CPMG at 800 and 900 MHz, 298 K, Trelax 30 ms, nuCPMG 66.7-1000 Hz: no dispersion for the core residues, and R2 at 1000 Hz is not raised relative to other residues, so neither exchange inside this pulsing range nor broadening from faster exchange is seen; exchange with a very small population or shift difference, or slower than the 30 ms delay, would not register

judgments.reason: With atRA bound the principal exchange is nearly fully quenched: the core residues show no dispersion and no raised R2 at high pulsing rates under the same buffer, temperature and concentration as the free protein.
judgments.function_link: The authors link the quenching to an Arg59-Gln74 hydrogen bond in the complex that locks betaD and the betaE-betaF loop into one unit.
